Portland borders Beaverton on the east, Hillsboro on the west and Tigard on the south, and the city lies in Washington County at the foot of the Tualatin Mountains. Its 97,494 residents in 2020 were 8.6 percent more than the 89,803 of 2010, which ranks it second in the county and seventh in Oregon.

The city has 13 neighborhoods, among them Central Beaverton, Denney Whitford, Raleigh West, Five Oaks, Triple Creek, Highland, South Beaverton, Vose and West Slope. People describe a house here by neighborhood and school boundary. The Beaverton School District covers most of the city, with portions in the Hillsboro School District and Portland Public Schools. Nike is the biggest employer, and work across the Silicon Forest corridor keeps rentals in demand.

A transfer tax applies to Beaverton sales, which is unusual in Oregon. The county takes $1 on every $1,000 of selling price. ORS 306.815 forbids most local transfer taxes yet spares those in place on March 31, 1997, and Washington County's version lives in Chapter 3.04 of its code.

Many transfers are exempt under the county's exemption form, but the claim has to be filed within 15 days of tendering the documents for recording.

  • Transfers by gift, devise or inheritance.
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure and court-ordered transfers in foreclosure or bankruptcy.
  • Transfers between spouses under a court order in a divorce.
  • Conveyances to or from a government entity.
  • Transfers with a selling price of $13,999 or less.

Have your escrow officer tell you who pays on your sale and which line of the settlement statement shows it.

Beaverton's bill comes from Washington County Assessment and Taxation. You can pay all at once or in thirds. The 3 percent discount for paying in full needs a November 15 postmark.

On the statement you will see Real Market Value (the estimated sale price on January 1) and Taxable Value (the smaller of market value and maximum assessed value), followed by education, general government, bond and local option levies. Back taxes from earlier years print there as well, and the oldest year is paid first. An asterisk means foreclosure.

Value appeals go to the Board of Property Tax Appeals by December 31. Measure 50 caps yearly assessed value growth at 3 percent. The county's sample tax statement page shows how to read each line.

Renters live in 52.5 percent of Beaverton's occupied homes and owners in 47.5 percent, so landlords make up a big share of sellers.

The governing law is ORS 90.427. Once the tenant is past year one, ending a tenancy for a sale generally takes an accepted offer from a buyer planning to live there, plus written notice 90 days or more ahead. One month's rent is due with the notice, unless the landlord owns four or fewer covered units.

Violations can cost three months' rent plus damages, which is why many landlords choose a buyer who keeps the lease going.

Rain totals about 39 inches a year, mostly October to April, with December the wettest month at 6.53 inches. Summers are dry. Snow barely registers at about 1.9 inches, and heat is the larger swing: July and August highs run near 80 degrees, and the record high is 115 degrees, set in June.

  • Gutters, downspouts and roof condition matter after a long wet season.
  • Attic insulation and cooling matter more as summer extremes show up.
  • Sloped lots in the hillier parts of the city can mean drainage and retaining wall questions. Elevation runs from about 132 feet to about 698 feet.

A lender's appraiser may flag a leaking roof or damp crawl space and stall a financed sale. Cash purchases skip that.

TriMet's MAX light rail has seven stations in the city: Elmonica/SW 170th Avenue, Merlo Road/SW 158th Avenue, Beaverton Creek, Millikan Way, Beaverton Central, Beaverton Transit Center and Sunset Transit Center. The Blue Line serves all seven and the Red Line serves the last two.

Beaverton Transit Center, TriMet's busiest, anchors the north end of WES commuter rail. US 26, the Sunset Highway, links the city to Portland, Hillsboro and the coast, and Oregon 217 runs south through Tigard to I-5.

A house a short walk from MAX is a different product than one needing a car for every errand, so tell buyers which you have.

A cash sale here follows the ordinary title and escrow path with the loan removed. Here is the usual order of events:

  1. You receive an offer and agree on a closing date.
  2. The title company searches the deed and any liens, including unpaid property tax.
  3. The escrow officer prepares the settlement statement, with the transfer tax, the split of the current year's property tax and any payoff shown on separate lines.
  4. You sign, the deed is recorded, and funds are released to you after the payoffs come out.

Because no lender is waiting on an appraisal, you can often pick the date, which helps if you are moving for work in the Silicon Forest corridor or settling an inherited house.

Beaverton grew from an 1840s farming settlement into a suburb incorporated in 1893. The Atfalati people lived here first, and the Hall family filed the first land claim in 1847. A plank road from Portland opened in 1860 and the first post office in 1872. The urban growth boundary has been expanded since, including the Cooper Mountain urban reserve area added in 2018, so newer subdivisions sit next to older neighborhoods and a seller should expect buyers to compare the two.

You are not required to fix the roof, drainage or cosmetics to sell as-is. The seller disclosure statute (ORS 105.462 to 105.490) may still govern what you tell a buyer, so check with the title company. With no lender's appraisal, a worn house can close without the repair demands that usually come with financing.

First collect your newest tax statement and note whether a tenant lives there. Then ask the escrow officer to show how the transfer tax and this year's property tax will be divided on the settlement statement. If taxes from earlier years are open, call 503-846-8801, the delinquent tax line, for the balance, and give it to the title company. Late installments are paid out of your proceeds at closing, oldest year first.

faqs.q: Does Beaverton have a transfer tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Under Washington County Code Chapter 3.04 the county takes $1 per $1,000 of selling price. Gifts, inheritance and some foreclosure transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: When is the Beaverton property tax deadline?
faqs.a: November 15. A full payment postmarked by then earns a 3 percent discount from Washington County, and thirds are also allowed.

faqs.q: Must I repair my Beaverton house before a cash sale?
faqs.a: No. Repairs are optional in an as-is sale, although Oregon's seller disclosure statute (ORS 105.462 to 105.490) may still apply.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Beaverton rental with a tenant in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Because ORS 90.427 limits ending a tenancy for a sale, a buyer who keeps the lease sidesteps the 90-day notice and the rent payment.

faqs.q: When do I appeal a Beaverton property value?
faqs.a: By December 31, to the Board of Property Tax Appeals. Call Washington County appraisal at 503-846-8826 with questions first.
